verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel a lightness in your chest these days and want to learn how to make it stay. Bhartrihari asks what generous austerity brought this freedom to wander at will, food without humiliation, good company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. You can rest in that gentle mind today, letting it stir only softly even as you look outward, and notice how this lightness already lives in your chest.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He is looking back at his own life. He has food that does not humiliate him. He wanders where he wants. He lives among good people. He learns things that bring calm. His mind barely stirs even when he looks at the world. He asks what generous austerity earned him all this. You carry a lightness in your chest right now. Bhartrihari asks what earned you this freedom and calm.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You mentioned a joy within and a wish to know it more deeply. Krishna tells Arjuna that one whose happiness, delight and light are all inside becomes one with Brahman and reaches lasting freedom. This inner glow you feel can keep growing as you explore it, without waiting for anything outside to change.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the yoga of knowledge. He describes the wise person who looks on all beings with an equal eye. Such a person is not lifted up by pleasure or brought down by pain. Their happiness lives inside them. Their delight lives inside them. Their light lives inside them. This yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman. The stillness you feel now has its own source. It does not depend on what comes next.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some pleasure tastes like nectar at first and poison in the end. Know which kind you're choosing.
verse_text.translation: The happiness that comes from contact of the senses with their objects, like nectar at first and like poison in the end, is called rajasic.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that pleasure born from the senses meeting their objects tastes like nectar at first, yet like poison in the end; he names this rajasic happiness. Since you feel a peaceful delight within and wish to know it more deeply, this verse points to the difference between that inner steadiness and the fleeting pull of outer stimulation. Notice, in your daily rhythm, where a craving for stimulation begins, and let the nectar-then-poison pattern show you which source you are touching.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Unhooked from outside pleasures, you find a joy within that doesn't run out.
verse_text.translation: One whose self is unattached to outer contacts finds the happiness that is in the self. Joined to Brahman by yoga, he enjoys undying happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that one unattached to outer contacts finds a happiness within that does not run out. This inner joy grows the more your delight rests on yourself alone. You already feel a quiet delight inside, so let that steady ground hold you today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: When the mind clears, sorrows start to dissolve, and understanding settles quickly.
verse_text.translation: In that clarity all sorrows come to an end; for one whose mind is clear, understanding soon becomes steady.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind clears, sorrows begin to dissolve and understanding settles quickly. This speaks to your peaceful state, where an inner delight already rests. Ground yourself today in that clear mind, letting understanding settle like still space.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some joy tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end. That joy is worth it.
verse_text.translation: That which is like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from the clarity of one's own understanding, is called sattvic happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that some joy tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from the clarity of your own understanding. Since a peaceful calm already lives within you, you could gently sit with one small practice today that feels difficult at the start, letting its deeper sweetness unfold.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse_text.line: A calm mind, gentleness, quiet, self-restraint and a clean heart: that is discipline of mind.
verse_text.translation: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint and purity of feeling: this is called austerity of the mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a calm mind, gentleness, quiet, self-restraint and a clean heart make up the discipline of mind. Since a quiet joy already lives within you, you could let your speech rest for a few minutes today and notice that inner stillness without seeking anything new.

story.title: Bhushunda
story.summary: The sage Vasishtha travelled to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who had watched whole ages of the world come and go and was still happy. Asked his secret, Bhushunda listed his habits. He didn't brood on the past or the future. He didn't fret about what he'd get next. Learning never made him proud. And he was glad when others were glad, and sad when they were sad.
story.lesson: A long, glad life comes from staying present, wanting little and staying kind.

days.reading: Bhushunda tells Vasishtha he stayed happy across endless ages because he did not brood on the past or fret about the future. This speaks to your peaceful inner state, showing that lasting joy grows when attention rests fully here. You can keep knowing that delight by letting go of what comes next.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Eating alone in the dining hall while others sit in tight groups is a heavy weight. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When you look around the room today, you might notice one shared thread in every face, a presence that stays close even when no one sits beside you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him about meditation and a settled mind. He tells him that if a person sees him in everything and sees everything in him, then Krishna is never lost to that person, and that person is never lost to Krishna. You are far from home and eating alone while others sit in groups. This idea says your connection is not broken just because you are sitting by yourself.

verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.

Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. In the quiet of your home, this means the presence you seek is not limited by distance or silence; it is already woven into the very air around you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is teaching him how to steady the mind through meditation. He tells Arjuna that a person who sees the divine presence in all things and sees all things within that presence will never be separated from it. The idea is that this mutual seeing creates a bond that distance or wandering thoughts cannot break. The presence you miss is not locked outside your door. It can meet you in the stillness of the rooms you share with your children.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna where the divine is found.
verse_text.line: The divine lives in the heart of every being, yours included.
verse_text.translation: The Lord dwells in the heart of every being, Arjuna, moving all beings by his power as if mounted on a machine.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, moving them all. That presence is in your heart too, right here in this flat and this city, not only back home or in a temple. When a day passes without another adult’s voice, you can stand on the fact that you are not alone in your own chest.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna who he is to every being.
verse_text.line: I am your goal, your support, your witness, your home, your shelter and your friend.
verse_text.translation: I am the goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the home, the refuge and the friend; the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house and the undying seed.

days.reading: In one verse Krishna lists what he is to every being: goal, support, witness, home (nivāsaḥ), shelter (śaraṇam) and friend (suhṛt). If you've been missing all of those, this verse names them together.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, briefly describing meditation and the peace it brings.
verse_text.line: The divine is the well-wisher of every being, you included. Knowing this, you find peace.
verse_text.translation: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the divine is the friend of all beings, your included, and knowing this brings peace. On days when you do not speak to another adult, this well-wisher remains present in the quiet. Rest in that steady presence here, now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Feel others' joy and pain as if they were your own. That is the highest practice.
verse_text.translation: One who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere, Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, is considered the highest yogi.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to feel others' joy and pain as if they were his own, calling this the highest practice. When your days pass without another adult's voice, you could quietly offer one small kindness to someone today, letting your attention move outward. In doing so, you echo the presence that has stayed with you since the first day.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse_text.line: Hate no one. Be friendly and kind, free of 'mine' and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving.
verse_text.translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the person dear to God hates no one, is friendly and compassionate, free from ego and possessiveness, steady through pain and joy, and forgiving. You could offer one kind word to a stranger today, letting go of who must reach out first. That small step is the practice itself, steady even when no reply comes back.

story.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
story.summary: Ram had lost his home, and his wife Sita had been taken. Sugriva, driven out by his brother, had lost his home and his wife too. They met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Then Sugriva brought out the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away. Ram broke down at the sight of them, and Sugriva, who had his own grief, comforted him: in trouble, think it through steadily, and lean on your friend.
story.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

days.reading: In the Kishkindha Kanda, Ram and Sugriva, both exiled and grieving, swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva comforts Ram with his own loss, showing that two people in trouble can carry each other. You wake in a new country without another adult to speak to; this story points to a shared fire where two broken people sit together and steady one another.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You have spent three years working from home and noticed you have no one, with your phone only buzzing for work. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer lights up at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but just keeps silent. That quiet stillness mirrors your own withdrawal today, as your days blur into work without connection.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Rama has stopped eating properly, stopped laughing, and sits alone. The attendant reports that Rama no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere weakness but the first stirring of deeper questions, provided someone helps the person through it. Your withdrawal after three years at home mirrors Rama's stillness. The silence is not a flaw. It is the ground where better questions can begin to form.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You are home with your mother while your wife is away and your children live in a hostel. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not killed when the body is. In your quiet house, this means the essence of the one you care for remains untouched by the silence around you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield of after Arjuna collapses in grief over fighting his own kin. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and declared he would rather die than kill his teachers and elders. Krishna replies that the true self within every person was never born and will never die. It does not perish when the body perishes. The self is eternal, ancient, and unchanging, so grief for the body is grief for a garment that is shed, not for what truly lives. Your mother is fading into silence while your wife is away and your children live elsewhere. This verse speaks to the part of her that outlasts the quiet room and the slow forgetting.

verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.

reading: You spend your days among colleagues and your off days alone in your room. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When your room feels empty, this view can meet you there: the one you seek is already present in the space around you, and you are already held within it.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to settle the mind through meditation. He tells the warrior that a person who sees him in every being and sees every being within him will never be separated from him, and he will never be separated from that person. The distance you feel between your work days and your empty room is not a break in connection. It is a place where you can learn to see the same presence in both.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant
verse_text.setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
verse_text.line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
verse_text.translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.

reading: You spend the day talking to people yet feel unknown. Rama's attendant tells King Dasharatha that the prince no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work, but simply keeps silent. Like that quiet withdrawal, your own stillness after constant conversation may be a sign that the noise no longer reaches you, leaving room for something unnamed to simply be there.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has stopped eating, stopped laughing, and sits alone. The attendant reports that the prince no longer reacts to jokes, takes no pleasure in things, and does not stay with his work. He simply keeps silent. Your own withdrawal after constant talking may be the first sign that the noise has stopped reaching you.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: After your fourth UPSC attempt, your courage is fading. Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like Arjuna, you too can let your weapons rest without forcing yourself forward. Your bow and arrows may also simply lie still today.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and sits in his chariot. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. The verse shows that even a great warrior can freeze when sorrow hits. It proposes that a breakdown is a real beginning, not a failure. After your fourth attempt, your courage is fading. Like Arjuna, you can set your weapons down without forcing the next step today.

verse_text.speaker: Rama's attendant

reading: You have poured everything into two businesses that closed, and now nothing stirs you. The Yoga Vasishtha records Rama's attendant describing the prince: he no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work; he just keeps silent. That quiet withdrawal speaks to your emptiness today. Let your stillness be enough, resting in the fact that you no longer force yourself to stay with what has already ended.
meaning: Rama's attendant speaks to King Dasharatha after the prince returns from a long pilgrimage. Sixteen-year-old Rama has quietly withdrawn. He stops eating, ignores his duties, and sits alone. The attendant reports that Rama no longer laughs at jokes, loses himself in pleasures, or stays with his work. He just keeps silent. The verse proposes that this loss of interest is not mere illness or weakness. It can be the start of asking better questions, provided someone helps the person through it. You poured everything into two businesses that closed, and now the silence where your drive used to be feels like proof that nothing will ever work for you.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You have been trying to lose weight for years and keep failing, and you have basically given up on yourself. In this verse, Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like Arjuna setting down his bow, your body may be resting after years of effort; today, that same seat of the chariot is simply where you are.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his weapons and collapsed in his chariot. He is paralyzed by grief and fear at the thought of fighting his own kin. Sanjaya reports that even the greatest warrior can freeze when his mind is overwhelmed. The verse shows that a breakdown is not a failure of strength but a human response to unbearable weight. After years of trying and failing, your body has settled into stillness. That stillness is not weakness. It is the honest result of carrying too much for too long.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.

reading: You feel defeated. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. When hope runs low after setbacks, sitting still with that weight is part of the path, not the end of it. Let your bow rest today, and stay in the chariot.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna stands among the armies, ready to fight his own kin. He is overcome by grief and fear. He drops his weapons and sinks onto the chariot seat. The verse records this collapse. It shows that even a mighty warrior can freeze when the cost of action feels too high. You are in that same seat, with the fight paused and the weight of defeat heavy on your chest.

reading: हर कोशिश नाकाम हो रही है, और अब हार मान लेने का मन कर रहा है। संजया कहते हैं कि अर्जुन ने युद्धभूमि में अपना धनुष गिराकर रथ पर बैठ गए, उनका मन शोक से भर गया। आज भी आप अपनी कोशिशों के बीच इसी तरह रुक सकते हैं; अपने काम के बीच एक पल रुककर अपने धनुष को नीचे रख दें, और बस वहीं बैठे रहें।
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra. On the battlefield, Arjuna has just laid down his weapons and collapsed in his chariot. He is paralyzed by grief and refuses to fight his own kin. The verse records this collapse. It shows that even a mighty warrior can freeze when sorrow overwhelms him. The Gita begins not with courage but with a breakdown.

Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and arrows. He sits in the chariot, overcome by grief and confusion. The verse records this moment of collapse. It shows that even a mighty warrior can freeze when the weight becomes too much. Your body has faced one setback after another, and now the knee surgery has failed too. You have stopped believing you will get better.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.

verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You keep waiting to restart your work each year, but something always gets in the way, and now hope feels gone. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Today, you too can lay down the weight of that yearly wait and simply sit where you are, with the bow set aside.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between the two armies. He sees his kin and teachers ready to die. Grief and fear grip him. He drops his bow and arrows. He sinks onto the chariot seat. He cannot move. The verse shows a collapse. It says even the strongest freeze when the cost becomes too clear. Your yearly restart has met the same wall again and again. The verse names that freeze without shame.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Poem 'Hold On Yet a While, Brave Heart', written to the Maharaja of Khetri.
verse_text.line: Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come.
verse_text.translation: If the sun by the cloud is hidden a bit, If the welkin shows but gloom, Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come. … Not a work will be lost, no struggle vain, Though hopes be blighted, powers gone; … Then hold on yet a while, brave soul, No good is e'er undone.

reading: You are carrying a land case that has dragged on for seven years, with every hearing postponed, and you have lost hope of ever getting justice. The verse says, 'Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come.' It speaks to your restlessness by trusting that no struggle is vain, even when the sky shows only gloom. You can hold on to this truth while you wait for the next hearing.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda wrote this poem to the Maharaja of Khetri, a friend facing hard times. He tells him that clouds may hide the sun for a while and the sky may show only gloom. Yet he says the victory is sure to come. No honest struggle is wasted, even when hopes fail and powers seem gone. The verse asks the listener to keep holding on a little longer. Your land case has dragged on for seven years and each hearing keeps slipping away. The verse asks you to trust that this long wait is not empty.

verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: After the fifth rejection on the same paper, you feel you do not have it in you to revise it again. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you can lay down what you have been carrying and simply sit with the weight of it today.

Overcome by grief and delusion, Arjuna lets his bow and arrows fall to the seat of his chariot. He sits down and refuses to fight. The verse records a moment of total collapse. Even a great warrior can freeze when the cost becomes too heavy. You are facing a fifth rejection on the same paper and you feel you have nothing left to give it another revision.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

meaning: Bali speaks this to himself. He is a demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day he sits by his window and sees that his days and nights repeat the same tasks. He feels that this endless loop mocks any thinking person. The verse proposes that when life feels like a closed circle, the way out is not to add more work but to master the mind that runs the loop. You are facing the same wall no matter how hard you push against it.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.

verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, overwhelmed by grief, put down his bow and sank onto the chariot seat. In your own running of things, you too can set down the weight of the next plan and simply sit, letting the bow rest where it is.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid out his grief and fear. He sees his kin arrayed against him and cannot bear to strike them down. His mind collapses under the weight of that love and dread. He lets his bow and arrows fall and sinks onto the chariot seat, too overwhelmed to continue. You are running your own thing and every plan has collapsed in a row. That collapse has left you feeling lost, as if the ground under your work has given way.

reading: After sixty rejections, you have set down your pen and stopped writing. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, the greatest archer, put down his bow and sat in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Like him, you may simply be too heavy to go on right now, and that collapse is where the teaching begins.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just laid down his bow and sat in his chariot. His mind is overwhelmed by grief. He refuses to fight because he cannot bear to kill his own kin. The verse records this collapse. It shows that even the greatest warrior can freeze when the weight becomes too much. You have stopped writing after sixty rejections. That freeze is not a failure of talent. It is the body and mind saying the load is too heavy right now.

verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting at a new company on the 1st after two years under a terrible manager, seeking a clean slate. Lakshman tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it; for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. Let that steadiness guide you as you step into this new chapter, carrying the hope you already feel into the work ahead.
meaning: At Lake Pampa, after Sita has been taken, Ram is overcome by grief. The beauty of spring only sharpens his sorrow. Lakshman steps in and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than it. For the person who holds it, nothing in the world is out of reach. After two years under a terrible manager, your hope for a clean slate is real. This verse names that hope as a strength you already carry into the new company.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You arrived in Toronto last month full of hope yet feeling scared. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and as hard to hold as the wind. Your thoughts may keep circling the newness around you, yet the same wind that resists the hand also carries the breath you draw in this city. Notice one steady breath tonight, and let the rest move as it will.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the field before battle. He admits that his mind jumps around and will not stay still. He says it is as hard to control as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is restless and strong. He adds that steady practice and letting go can slowly train it. You are in a place where hope and fear share the same room. Arjuna names the same restlessness you feel after a move.

verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

Savitri tells her father-in-law, "I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end." As you begin this new chapter tomorrow, let that same resolve guide your hands in the soil and your decisions on the land.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her father-in-law, after she learns her husband Satyavan will die within three days. She has begun a hard three night vow to face death itself. She tells him not to be distressed. She says the vow was begun with determination, and determination alone will carry it to the end. She means that steady resolve can sustain a promise even when fear would make someone drop it. You are leaving a long corporate career to begin your own farm tomorrow, and you carry that same resolve into the unknown.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Don't abandon work that suits you just because it has flaws. Every undertaking has some, like fire has smoke.
verse_text.translation: One should not give up the work suited to one's nature, Kaunteya, even if it has faults; for all undertakings are clouded by faults, as fire is by smoke.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that every undertaking is clouded by faults, just as fire is by smoke, so do not abandon work suited to your nature simply because it has flaws. As you begin this first job abroad and fly to Doha, expect small imperfections to appear, but let that steadiness carry you through the week ahead.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Without self-control it's hard. With sincere effort and the right means, it's within reach.
verse_text.translation: Yoga is hard to reach for one whose self is uncontrolled, in my view. But one whose self is controlled and who strives can reach it by the right means.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga is hard for one whose mind is uncontrolled, but reachable for one who strives by the right means. As you begin your first job abroad and fly to Doha, this steadiness gives you ground to stand on. The unfamiliar path feels hard because it is new, yet sincere effort makes it within reach.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: So keep doing the work that needs doing, well and without clinging. That's how you rise.
verse_text.translation: Therefore, always do the work that has to be done, without attachment; by working without attachment a person reaches the highest.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to keep doing the work that needs doing, well and without clinging, because that is how one rises. As you settle into your first job abroad, this steadiness gives you ground to stand on while the newness fades. Let your focus rest on doing today’s tasks well, without obsessing over how the whole journey will turn out.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Cut the doubt in your heart with clear understanding, then stand up and act.
verse_text.translation: Therefore, cutting with the sword of knowledge this doubt in your heart born of ignorance, take refuge in yoga, and stand up, Bharata.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to cut the doubt in his heart with the sword of clear understanding, then stand up and act. As you begin this new job abroad, doubt may visit you, but you do not have to wait for it to leave. You could write down one fact you know about this role today, then take the first step.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna, as Time, tells Arjuna the outcome is already set and urges him to act.
verse_text.line: It's already set in motion. Rise and do your part; be the instrument.
verse_text.translation: Therefore stand up and win glory; conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. They have already been slain by me; be merely the instrument, ambidextrous archer.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the larger outcome is already in motion and urges him to rise and play his part, being merely the instrument. As you fly to Doha for your first job abroad, you could embrace this by showing up fully for one small task today, trusting you are part of something bigger.

story.title: Satyakama Jabala
story.summary: Young Satyakama wanted to study, but he didn't know his father's lineage. He told the teacher exactly what his mother had told him. The teacher accepted him for that honesty and handed him four hundred weak, thin cows to look after. Satyakama said he wouldn't come back until they were a thousand. He spent years in the forest, and returned with a thousand cows and a mind that nature itself had taught.
story.lesson: Start honestly, start small, and stay with it.

days.reading: Satyakama tells his teacher he does not know his father's lineage, and the teacher accepts his honesty, giving him four hundred weak cows to tend. You are beginning a new chapter far from home, and this story shows that starting with what you actually know, and with a small, fragile step, can grow into something far larger than you began. You carry those thin cows with you into Doha, and you will not return until they have become a thousand.

He tells Ram that enthusiasm holds the greatest power of all. For the person who carries it, no task in the world lies beyond reach. You left one home to begin again in a place you do not yet know. That shift asks for a quiet kind of energy, and this verse names where it comes from.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You registered your company today and feel the real journey has begun. Savitri tells her father-in-law, "I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end." Your resolve now mirrors hers: let that same steady will guide your company through what lies ahead.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her father-in-law, after she learns her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a hard three-night vow to face death itself. Savitri's words meet the moment your own resolve hardens into something that must last.
